blocks.text: A 27-year-old keen runner finishes a hot half-marathon, drinks little, and by evening is rolling on the floor with pain that comes in waves from her left loin to the groin. She cannot lie still. Pain, haematuria and a dehydrated kidney: a ureteric stone is the commonest reason for this picture, and an infected one behind it is the commonest reason for it to become a surgical emergency.

blocks.markdown: **Urinary stones: how they form and where they lodge.** Stones form when urine is supersaturated with stone-forming salts, particularly when volume is low, urine is concentrated or pH is abnormal. Calcium oxalate stones are commonest; others are calcium phosphate, uric acid (acid urine; gout, high purine intake), struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate; urease-producing organisms such as *Proteus*, which cause infection stones and staghorn calculi) and cystine (inherited cystinuria). A stone moves from the kidney down the ureter and may lodge at three narrow points: the **pelviureteric junction**, the **pelvic brim** (where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels) and the **vesicoureteric junction**, the narrowest.

blocks.title: Ureteric (renal) colic
blocks.text: Severe, intermittent loin-to-groin pain caused by acute ureteric obstruction and spasm as a stone passes. Pain radiates toward the groin, testis or labia as the stone descends, and a stone at the vesicoureteric junction may cause urinary frequency and urgency. The patient is **restless and writhes**, unlike peritonitis where the patient lies still. There is often nausea and vomiting and haematuria (visible or on dipstick), though its absence does not exclude a stone.

blocks.markdown: **Imaging.** In an adult with suspected renal colic, a low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder (CT KUB) is the reference investigation and, per NICE guidance, should be performed within 24 hours; it detects stones of all compositions and shows hydronephrosis and alternative diagnoses. Ultrasound is used in pregnancy and children, and shows hydronephrosis but visualises ureteric stones poorly. A plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) sees only radio-opaque stones (calcium-containing and, less well, struvite and cystine), but **uric acid stones are radiolucent**. In people over about 60 presenting with first-time loin pain, an abdominal aortic aneurysm must be considered before assuming colic. Check urine dipstick, FBC, CRP, U&E and creatinine, and calcium; urinalysis and pregnancy tests are part of initial assessment.

rows: Alkaline urine, renal tubular acidosis, hyperparathyroidism
Acidic urine, gout, high purine intake

blocks.title: Worked example: a stone that may pass
blocks.prompt: A 40-year-old man has a 5 mm stone in the distal left ureter on CT with mild hydronephrosis. His pain is controlled with oral analgesia, urine is not infected, temperature is normal and creatinine is at baseline. Decide.

steps.text: The stone is small and distal, so spontaneous passage is likely (smaller and more distal stones pass more often; exact figures vary between series).
There are no markers of urgent intervention: no fever or infection, normal renal function, a single functioning kidney is not involved and pain is controlled.

Plan: oral analgesia (NSAID first-line unless contraindicated, check BNF and NICE), antiemetic, fluids as tolerated, strain urine, clear safety-netting (return at once for fever, vomiting preventing oral intake, uncontrolled pain or reduced urine output), and outpatient urology follow-up or imaging to confirm passage.
If the stone does not pass within the follow-up period or symptoms persist, offer ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy.

blocks.answer: Conservative management with analgesia, safety-netting and follow-up; intervention only if indicated.

blocks.title: The obstructed infected kidney
blocks.text: A stone (or other obstruction) with **infection upstream** produces pus under pressure (pyonephrosis) and can cause bacteraemia and septic shock within hours. Suspect it with fever, rigors, loin pain, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion or raised inflammatory markers, particularly in the elderly, diabetic or immunosuppressed, and in a solitary kidney. **It is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression** (percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent) **plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and resuscitation**. Definitive stone removal is delayed until sepsis resolves, because manipulating an infected obstructed system can precipitate septic shock.

blocks.caption: MAP in mmHg; urine output is often targeted at about 0.5 mL/kg/h or more in sepsis monitoring (check local protocol).

blocks.title: Worked example: a septic obstructed kidney
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg, 66-year-old woman with a known 9 mm stone presents with fever 39.2 C, rigors, heart rate 126 and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. After 2 hours she has passed 30 mL urine. Assess and manage.

steps.text: MAP = 60 + (100 - 60)/3 = 73.3 mmHg; perfusion is borderline but the heart rate and fever show systemic inflammation.
Urine output = 30 mL / (70 kg x 2 h) = 0.21 mL/kg/h, below the commonly used target of about 0.5 mL/kg/h, indicating poor renal or systemic perfusion or an obstruction.

Start sepsis management immediately: oxygen as needed, IV access, blood cultures and lactate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per local guidance within the first hour, IV fluids, and close monitoring (check BNF and protocol).
Arrange urgent imaging and decompression of the obstructed system (nephrostomy or stent) by urology/interventional radiology; defer stone treatment until infection has cleared.

blocks.answer: Obstructed infected kidney with sepsis: resuscitate, give antibiotics and urgently decompress.

blocks.markdown: **Options for stone management.** Choice depends on stone size, location, composition, symptoms, anatomy and patient factors. *Observation with analgesia* suits small, distal, uncomplicated ureteric stones. *Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy* (ESWL) fragments stones from outside the body with focused shockwaves, and is best for smaller upper-tract stones; it is avoided in pregnancy and uncorrected coagulopathy. *Ureteroscopy* passes a fine scope retrograde, fragmenting the stone with laser (holmium) or retrieving it with a basket, often with a temporary stent. *Percutaneous nephrolithotomy* (PCNL) removes large renal stones (generally above about 2 cm) via a track into the kidney. Open or laparoscopic surgery is rare. Decompression by stent or nephrostomy treats obstruction and infection but not the stone.

blocks.title: Preventing recurrence
blocks.text: Recurrence is common. General advice: drink enough to keep urine dilute (often a target urine output of at least 2 to 2.5 litres a day), reduce salt and excess animal protein, maintain a normal dietary calcium intake (restricting it can increase oxalate absorption), and manage body weight. Further metabolic evaluation (serum calcium, urate, urine pH and 24-hour urine collection) is used for recurrent or high-risk formers; drug therapy (for example thiazides, potassium citrate, allopurinol) is guided by the metabolic findings and BNF/specialist advice.

points: Ureteric colic is severe loin-to-groin pain with a restless patient and haematuria; low-dose non-contrast CT KUB is the standard imaging, and uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain radiographs.
A stone with infection behind it is an emergency: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent decompression by nephrostomy or stent come before definitive stone treatment.
Stone treatment is by size and site: observation with analgesia, ESWL, ureteroscopy with laser, PCNL for large renal stones; prevention rests on fluids, diet and metabolic evaluation.
Doses and antibiotics must be checked against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with sudden severe right loin pain radiating to the groin, vomiting and restlessness. Urine dipstick shows blood. He is afebrile with normal observations. Which is the most appropriate imaging?

options.text: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder

questions.correctOptionText: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the standard investigation in adults.
distractorRationale.b: Misses radiolucent stones and is insensitive.
distractorRationale.c: Rarely used now; CT is preferred.
distractorRationale.d: Not appropriate for urinary tract stones.

questions.explanation: Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB detects stones of all compositions, shows hydronephrosis and identifies alternative diagnoses, and should be available within 24 hours of suspected renal colic. Ultrasound or other modalities are used in pregnancy and children.

questions.stem: On a plain abdominal radiograph, a uric acid stone appears radio-opaque and is easily seen.
questions.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent and therefore invisible on plain radiographs, although they show on CT and sometimes on ultrasound with shadowing. Calcium-containing stones are radio-opaque.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman known to have a stone in the right ureter presents with right loin pain, rigors, a temperature of 39.4 C, heart rate 128/min and blood pressure 86/48 mmHg. CT shows a 7 mm stone with hydronephrosis. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics with urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent
Discharge with oral analgesia and tamsulosin
Wait 48 hours for the stone to pass

questions.correctOptionText: IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics with urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent

distractorRationale.c: Manipulating an infected obstructed system can cause septic shock.

questions.explanation: Stone obstruction with infection and haemodynamic compromise is a urological emergency. Resuscitation and antibiotics are started at once and the obstructed system is decompressed; the stone is treated definitively after the infection has settled.

questions.stem: A patient with an obstructed infected kidney has blood pressure 82/46 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg using MAP = diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = 82 - 46 = 36 mmHg, so MAP = 46 + 36/3 = 58.0 mmHg. This is below the commonly used sepsis target of at least 65 mmHg, supporting urgent resuscitation.

questions.stem: An 82 kg man with septic obstruction passes 120 mL of urine in 4 hours. Calculate his urine output in mL per kg per hour.
questions.explanation: Urine output = 120 / (82 x 4) = 120 / 328 = 0.37 mL/kg/h. This is below the commonly used target of about 0.5 mL/kg/h, which suggests under-perfusion or ongoing obstruction.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a single 2.8 cm stone in the right renal pelvis with no infection. Which treatment is most appropriate?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: large renal stones are generally treated percutaneously.
distractorRationale.b: Unlikely to pass and may obstruct.
distractorRationale.c: Medical expulsive therapy is for small ureteric stones.

questions.explanation: Renal stones above about 2 cm are generally treated with percutaneous nephrolithotomy, because ESWL and ureteroscopy are less likely to clear a large burden in one procedure. Choice is individualised by stone size, composition and patient factors.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with calcium oxalate stones asks how to reduce recurrence. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.text: Drink enough to keep urine output high, reduce salt and maintain normal dietary calcium
Restrict fluids to reduce urine production
Take large doses of vitamin C supplements

questions.correctOptionText: Drink enough to keep urine output high, reduce salt and maintain normal dietary calcium

distractorRationale.b: Can increase oxalate absorption and stone risk.

questions.explanation: A high fluid intake, reduced sodium and animal protein, and normal dietary calcium are the mainstays of prevention. Calcium restriction is not advised as it increases oxalate absorption.

questions.stem: A stone passing down the ureter may lodge at any of three anatomical narrowings. Which of the following is the narrowest point, where stones most often become impacted?

options.text: The mid-ureter in the psoas muscle

distractorRationale.c: Not a recognised site of narrowing.
distractorRationale.d: This is the urethra, not the ureter.

questions.explanation: The ureter has three narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the vesicoureteric junction, the narrowest. Stones frequently lodge at the last, causing groin pain and urinary frequency.

questions.stem: Outline the options for managing urinary tract stones and explain how stone size and position influence the choice.
markingGuide: Observation with analgesia (NSAID first-line unless contraindicated) for small, distal, uncomplicated stones; safety-netting and follow-up
ESWL for smaller renal and proximal ureteric stones
Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy for ureteric stones and some renal stones; stent if needed
PCNL for large renal stones (above about 2 cm) and staghorn calculi
Decompression (stent or nephrostomy) for obstruction with infection, solitary kidney or AKI
questions.explanation: A strong answer links the intervention to stone characteristics and patient factors, and recognises decompression as a separate emergency measure rather than stone treatment.

questions.stem: Explain why an obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency and outline its management.
markingGuide: Obstruction plus infection leads to pyonephrosis, pressure and bacteraemia, risking septic shock and renal loss
Features: fever, rigors, loin pain, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion, raised markers; higher risk in diabetes, elderly, solitary kidney
Resuscitation: oxygen, IV fluids, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour (per BNF/local protocol)
Urgent decompression by nephrostomy or retrograde stent after imaging
Definitive stone treatment delayed until infection resolves
Monitor urine output, renal function and lactate
questions.explanation: The marker looks for the pathophysiological link between obstruction, infection and sepsis, the combination of resuscitation with decompression, and the principle of delaying definitive treatment.
